clinicalPearls: A lateral neck swelling arising from incomplete regression of the embryological branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus, most commonly from the second cleft
The typical location is along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the upper to mid neck
It often becomes clinically apparent in older children or young adults, sometimes enlarging after an upper respiratory infection
Anomalies may take the form of a cyst, sinus, or fistula; a fistulous opening at the lower neck that discharges may indicate a tract to the pharynx
Infected cysts present as tender, inflamed, sometimes fluctuant masses and should have infection controlled before elective excision
Ultrasound is a useful first-line study, with cross-sectional imaging helping to define the tract before surgery
Definitive management is complete surgical excision of the cyst and any associated tract to prevent recurrence
In adults, a persistently cystic lateral neck mass should raise suspicion of a cystic nodal metastasis rather than a benign branchial cyst
reference.pathophysiology: The branchial apparatus of clefts, arches, and pouches contributes to head and neck development and normally regresses. Failure of obliteration of a cleft or its associated structures leaves an epithelial-lined remnant that can form a cyst, a blind-ending sinus, or a complete fistula connecting skin to pharynx. Second cleft anomalies characteristically pass between the internal and external carotid arteries toward the tonsillar fossa. Retained secretions distend the cyst, and communication with the pharynx or skin predisposes to recurrent infection.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic metastatic lymph node (in older patients)
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound to characterise the cystic lesion
CT or MRI to map the tract and its relationship to the carotid vessels before excision
Fine-needle aspiration when malignancy or nodal metastasis is a concern, particularly in adults
Fistulography in cases with a discharging sinus or fistula
Inflammatory markers and cultures if infection is present
redFlags: A cystic lateral neck mass in an older patient that may represent metastatic squamous carcinoma
Acute infection with abscess formation requiring drainage
Rapid enlargement or solid components suggesting an alternative or malignant diagnosis
Airway or vascular compromise from a large or deep lesion
reference.prognosis: Benign branchial anomalies have an excellent prognosis after complete excision, with recurrence mainly seen when a tract is incompletely removed or when surgery is undertaken during active infection. Long-term outlook is worse only when a presumed cyst proves to be a cystic malignancy.
pitfalls: Assuming a lateral neck cyst in an adult is benign without excluding malignancy
Incomplete excision of the tract, leading to recurrence
Operating during acute infection, increasing the risk of incomplete removal and complications
Injuring adjacent nerves or vessels because the tract's course was not defined preoperatively
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Complete surgical excision of the cyst and any sinus or fistulous tract for cure
Antibiotic treatment and control of infection before elective surgery, avoiding excision during active inflammation
Ultrasound with cross-sectional imaging to map the tract relative to the carotid vessels before excision
Fine-needle aspiration to exclude malignancy or nodal metastasis, particularly in adults
Meticulous complete tract excision to prevent recurrence
Referral to paediatric surgery or otolaryngology
